data.title: Defa opens Asean opportunities for Singapore SMEs, but many may not be ready
data.description:
[MANILA] A new Asean digital trade pact could make it easier for Singapore’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to expand across the region, but many may lack the resources and expertise to take full advantage of it.

Business leaders said the agreement could help firms enter new markets and manage regional operations more efficiently, although smaller companies may struggle to translate its provisions into commercial gains.

The Asean Digital Economy Framework Agreement (Defa), signed in Manila on Nov 14, aims to reduce digital trade barriers across the 11-member grouping, including by facilitating cross-border payments, electronic trade documentation and data flows.

Carmen Chan, deputy head of global transaction banking at OCBC, said SMEs face fragmented payment systems, currencies, regulations and documentation processes when doing business across Asean.

They may also lack visibility over foreign exchange conversion rates, when suppliers will receive payments and whether the full amount will be received.

“For SMEs with lean finance and treasury teams, managing these complexities across multiple markets can become a significant operational and administrative burden as they expand regionally,” she said.

Uneven legal recognition of electronic trade documents also means some transactions still require physical paperwork, slowing processing and increasing costs. Greater interoperability could ease these burdens and facilitate quicker access to trade financing, Chan said.

Making sense of Defa

But understanding how to make use of such agreements remains a challenge for smaller businesses.

Speaking to Singapore journalists at the conclusion of the 49th Asean Summit on Tuesday (Nov 17), Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said Singapore would work with other Asean governments to raise awareness of Defa and develop practical guides for businesses.

He noted that companies often struggled to understand how existing free trade agreements applied to them.

“What does it mean for me as a business? How do I make use of this?” he said, recounting questions businesses commonly raise.

A survey of 184 firms across eight Asean markets found that 35 per cent were unfamiliar with Defa, while another 49 per cent knew about it but had not assessed its implications. Only 4 per cent had an action plan.

The findings, from the 2026 Asean Business Outlook Survey conducted by the American Chamber of Commerce in Singapore, Accenture and Google, broadly reflected the experience of Ang Yuit, president of the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises.

He said the difficulty went beyond understanding an agreement. Businesses also needed to interpret its provisions, assess their relevance to individual operations and work out how to act on them.

That could require a dedicated internationalisation team, something smaller companies may not have the resources for, Ang noted.

Maneesh Tripathi, senior adviser to SME Centre@SICCI (Singapore Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry), agreed.

“They don’t have the manpower,” he said, noting that SME owners were often occupied with paying salaries, managing expenses and keeping their businesses running.

“They also do not have deep pockets to make a mistake,” he added, noting that finding reliable overseas partners was another major hurdle that trade agreements alone could not resolve.

Guna Chellappan, immediate past co-chair of SGTech’s AI, Cloud & Data Chapter, similarly observed that many Singapore businesses tended to wait until the practical implications of new agreements became clearer before acting.

Greater opportunities, more competition

While Defa could make regional expansion easier, it could also intensify competition for Singapore SMEs, which already face pressure from overseas businesses.

Tripathi warned that digital service providers in lower-cost markets such as Indonesia and Vietnam could offer similar services more cheaply than Singapore firms. He cited digital payment platforms as an example, where lower operating costs could translate into more competitive transaction fees.

“There will be severe competition,” he said, noting that startups and SMEs could come under pressure.

Ang raised another concern: easier cross-border payments could encourage Singapore consumers to spend more overseas, particularly if transaction fees and exchange rates become more attractive.

Singapore already has payment linkages with countries including Malaysia and Thailand, but more seamless transactions across Asean could encourage further overseas spending.

Domestic merchants could benefit from spending by incoming tourists, although Ang cautioned that the gains might be uneven. “The benefit to the local businesses here may not be that strong, or it will be uneven,” he said.

Chan similarly acknowledged that greater digital integration could lower barriers for regional businesses seeking to serve customers in new markets.

“In that sense, Defa is a double-edged sword: it can create new growth opportunities for Singapore SMEs while also increasing competitive pressures,” she said.

Asked by The Business Times about competition from lower-cost regional rivals, PM Wong acknowledged the concerns but said businesses would have to adapt.

“The competition is going to be there whether we like it or not. Companies will have to embrace the competition,” he said. The government would provide more support to help SMEs transform their operations, improve productivity and use digital and artificial intelligence tools to compete more effectively, he added.

Chellappan pointed to Singapore’s technological capabilities, infrastructure and regulatory environment as advantages that local businesses could draw on despite their higher operating costs.

Still, SMEs would need help navigating the opportunities available.

Ang suggested clearer government channels through which businesses could seek assistance when encountering difficulties applying trade agreements overseas.

Chellappan favoured a single coordinating organisation to guide SMEs through the available support schemes, rather than leaving them to approach several agencies.

Tripathi took a different view, saying the government had already done “considerable work” educating businesses. Trade associations should now play a greater role, he said, suggesting briefings before overseas trade missions and regular explanations of trade agreements in their newsletters.

For Singapore SMEs, understanding Defa will be only part of the task.

“Businesses will still need to differentiate themselves through product quality, innovation, customer service and specialised expertise to compete effectively in a larger and more interconnected Asean marketplace,” Chan said.

data.title: Singapore is winning the HQ race. Is it winning the leadership race?
data.description:
SINGAPORE now hosts about 1,030 foreign headquarters, up from roughly 770 in 2019. Over the same period, the resident professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) working in them grew by less than 8 per cent, from 12,700 to 13,700, as The Straits Times reported recently.

The explanation on offer is reassuring. A regional headquarters today, one adviser told the paper, is often “a leaner set-up focused on senior decision-making”, while operational roles move to cheaper markets.

That may well be true. The problem is that nobody measures it. Singapore counts its headquarters well. It does not yet count what they decide.

What the numbers miss

The PME figures also leave out foreign professionals, so headcount was never the right test of a headquarters. What matters is whether decision-making authority grew alongside the count. On that, the published figures are silent.

The Economic Strategy Review, published in June 2026, wants Singapore’s own companies to keep “headquarters, strategy and decision-making” functions here as they expand abroad, and foreign investors to make Singapore “a critical node” in their operations.

A headquarters, in the sense that counts for an economy, is where decisions are made. For a startup that re-domiciles here, that means where its chief executive and senior team sit.

Flipkart, founded in Bengaluru and serving customers across India, was incorporated in Singapore for 15 years before completing its move back to India in March 2026, ahead of a planned listing.

Throughout that time, Flipkart’s operations stayed in India alongside its executive leadership, while the Singapore headquarters focused on raising capital.

Grab offers a counter-example. Founded in Malaysia, the startup uses its Singapore headquarters as a control centre to manage localised teams across eight South-east Asian markets.

For a multinational’s regional headquarters, the test is narrower. In matrix organisations, few regional heads own every budget.

Even as global head offices hold ultimate control over bigger budgets, genuine regional headquarters can exert strategic influence and anchor a high-value ecosystem of professional services. For this, local leaders require sufficient autonomy.

Can the leaders here approve investment in the region, hire their own team and stop a project without needing a flight to the head office?

The Swiss mirror

Switzerland, where I am based, shows how control can move while the address stays.

Switzerland’s two federal technology universities, ETH in Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne, each produced a record number of new companies in 2025. But Swiss investors supplied at most about 13 per cent of later-stage capital for local startups that year, the Swiss Scale-Up Report 2026 found.

Growth money comes mostly from abroad.

Nexthink, an EPFL spin-off, is a Swiss success story. It still names Lausanne as one of its two headquarters. Its founder and chief executive, however, lives in the Boston area, and in October 2025, the company agreed to sell a majority stake to the American investor Vista Equity Partners.

On paper, Nexthink remains a Swiss-headquartered company. Where its biggest decisions are now taken is a different question.

That is also the risk Singapore faces: A company can maintain its official address in the country long after its true centre of decision-making has moved abroad.

When authority stays at home

In one executive search I handled, a company hired a Singapore-based leader for their understanding of the Asean market.

Yet headquarters, thousands of kilometres away, controlled the expansion budgets, assuming that what worked at home would work in the region.

The hire left for a direct competitor after 14 months, telling me that the lack of decision-making authority was the reason. The company had recruited local judgment but left it little room to act.

Retaining control overseas cost the company the local expertise it had recruited for its regional hub.

Singapore may get the leadership role, but does the authority move with it?

It can go the other way. In October 2026, Nike said the leadership team for a combined Asia-Pacific and Greater China region would be based in Singapore from fiscal year 2028, with some roles moving from its US headquarters.

Whether moves such as that bring real decision rights with them is exactly what Singapore should be tracking.

Closing the gap

Three changes would help.

First, measure authority as well as addresses. Singapore already counts its foreign headquarters and the resident PMEs in them. It could also survey whether those headquarters hold budget and hiring authority for the region, and publish the results in aggregate.

For startups that re-domicile, it could track where the chief executive and senior team are based.

Second, tie incentives to actual decision-making rights.

Today’s international headquarters award counts skilled jobs and local spending. Managing the group from Singapore is one qualifying activity among several, but it is not required.

As Singapore reviews its incentives for the era of the global minimum tax, awards could give weight to whether a regional chief executive or finance chief is a tax resident here and holds the regional budget.

Third, companies should move authority along with the address.

A startup that re-domiciles for capital or neutrality, while keeping every senior role elsewhere, has bought an address. A multinational that hires a regional leader here but signs off every budget at home has bought a title.

Businesses that put real decisions here, give regional leaders real budgets, and hire the next layer locally get what the address was meant to bring: proximity to regional customers, a deeper pool of talent and credibility with the investors who now concentrate their money here.

Singapore has already won the argument about where companies in this region want to be registered. The harder contest is about where they are run from.

To stay the region’s launchpad in 2027 and beyond, Singapore should count not only its headquarters, but also what they are allowed to decide.

The writer is the founder of Gunia Consulting, an advisory and executive search firm for organisation and leadership, with mandates in Europe and Asia, including Singapore. He is based in Zurich.

Views expressed here are his own. He used AI tools for research and editing before submitting the draft.

data.title: Malaysiaâs October CPI rises 1.9% y/y, slightly lower than forecast
data.description:
[KUALA LUMPUR] Malaysia’s consumer price index (CPI) rose 1.9 per cent from a year earlier in October, government data showed on Thursday (Nov 19).

The rise was slightly lower than the 2 per cent growth forecast by 13 economists in a Reuters poll. The index rose 1.8 per cent in September. REUTERS

data.title: PM Wong urges Apec leaders to keep Asia-Pacific from splitting into âcompeting economic blocsâ
data.description:
[SHENZHEN] The world may be entering an era of globalisation that is more fragmented and contested than before, but the Asia-Pacific should avoid becoming divided into “competing economic blocs”, said Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong.

Instead, the region can choose to remain open, connected and outward-looking, he said on Thursday (Nov 19).

“By working together, we can ensure that our region continues to be an engine of growth and prosperity for the world,” said PM Wong.

He was speaking at a plenary session on the second and final day of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) Economic Leaders’ Meeting in China’s southern tech and manufacturing hub of Shenzhen.

Remarkable transformation

Shenzhen was little more than a fishing village before it was designated China’s first special economic zone in 1980. 

Today, it is a megacity, with more than 18 million residents as at end-2025, and an economy a quarter larger than neighbouring Hong Kong’s. 

PM Wong praised the city’s “remarkable transformation” and said it shows what openness, innovation and economic cooperation can achieve. 

“It is also a reflection of the wider Asia-Pacific success story – a region that has prospered by opening up and connecting with the world,” he said.

Apec comprises 21 member economies, including several Asean member states such as Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand, as well as the US, Russia and China, whose leaders were present at the summit.

PM Wong’s call for stronger cooperation echoed his remarks as the incoming Asean chair at the closing ceremony for the bloc’s 49th summit on Tuesday in Manila, where he spoke about deepening economic integration among the grouping’s members while remaining open to the rest of the world.

New realities

PM Wong urged leaders at the Apec gathering to “adapt to these new realities” of global fragmentation and said the forum has an important role to play in keeping the region united.

In outlining how it could do so, he stressed the importance of keeping the Asia-Pacific open and connected.

While Apec has trade agreements such as the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), PM Wong said “we should not stop there”.

Rather, effort should be made to “build on these agreements and take concrete steps towards Apec’s vision of a free trade area of the Asia-Pacific”.

He added that these arrangements should remain “open and inclusive”, and reinforce rather than divide the wider trading system.

A general review of the RCEP is scheduled to take place in 2027. 

He added that Apec must continue to support reforms to strengthen the World Trade Organization (WTO) and uphold a rules-based multilateral trading system.

PM Wong acknowledged that reaching consensus among all economies will be increasingly difficult.

“But that should not become an excuse for inaction,” he said.

He pointed to plurilateral initiatives at the WTO, such as the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement and the E-commerce Agreement, as examples of how willing partners can make progress.

He said newer initiatives such as the Green Economy Partnership Agreement and the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership can also help develop innovative approaches to emerging opportunities.

“We should pursue a more flexible and pragmatic approach to multilateralism,” said the prime minister. “Allow willing partners to move ahead, demonstrate what works, and keep the door open for others to join when ready.”

Working together on AI

On artificial intelligence, PM Wong said there has been much public discussion about the competition for leadership position, as well as who has the best chips or models.

While “some of that is inevitable”, he said there is also much scope to work closely together on important issues such as AI safety and the responsible use of the technology.

He said Apec can help by supporting AI adoption among small and medium-sized enterprises, fostering investment in resilient AI infrastructure, and equipping workers with the skills to benefit from these technologies. 

The Apec Business Advisory Council (Abac) recently released a report that provides suggestions to governments on how they could help companies adopt AI by setting common standards for data sharing, clarifying regulation and reimbursement rules, and investing in workforce skills and digital infrastructure. 

Furthermore, the prime minister said Apec must ensure that economic cooperation delivers real benefits for businesses and people.

One example he cited was the Apec Centre of Excellence for Paperless Trade, conceived by Singapore and Australia together with Abac.

The initiative, he said, aims to make it easier for businesses to exchange trade documents electronically across borders, reducing paperwork and costs, and making it easier for smaller companies to enter new markets. 

“Ultimately, Apec’s success will be judged not by the declarations we issue, but by whether businesses find it easier to trade, workers have better opportunities, and our people see improvements in their lives,” said PM Wong.

Earlier in the day, Chinese President Xi Jinping had announced in opening remarks that China would provide US$20 million to support “Apec’s practical cooperation”.

Without going into details, he said in Mandarin that China would establish a centre for Asia Pacific Community Studies in Shenzhen to conduct policy research and exchanges and “provide intellectual support”.

China will also set up institutions to facilitate cooperation in areas such as digital technology, cross-border data flow, clean energy, and the development of SMEs, to “contribute to the innovation-driven and green growth in the Asia-Pacific”, Xi added.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Bank of Japan chief plays down soft consumption data, signals near-term rate hike
data.description:
[TOKYO] Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said the central bank will keep raising interest rates and projected consumer spending will recover from a soft patch, bolstering the case for another hike in borrowing costs as soon as next month.

Ueda also signalled that the BOJ is being vigilant about the inflationary impact of the weak yen, saying the currency’s slide may cause an inflation overshoot by boosting prices for a wide range of goods.

“We are mindful of the risk that rising crude oil prices and yen declines, if they persist, could hurt households’ real income and weigh on consumption more than expected,” Ueda told parliament on Thursday (Nov 19).

The yen’s weakness has been a headache for Japanese policymakers as it boosts the cost of raw material imports, pushing up prices of food and daily necessities.

It has dropped 1.8 per cent for the year to date to trade near 160 per dollar — a level seen as heightening the chance of currency intervention — with the dollar bought on growing prospects the US Federal Reserve will raise rates next month.

A majority of analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to also raise interest rates in December and follow up with another by end-March.

Firms more active in passing on costs

Some analysts have focused on whether a drop in private consumption seen in third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) data could affect the pace and timing of future rate hikes.

Ueda said consumer spending was resilient as a whole, with the drop seen in third-quarter GDP data resulting from the rising cost of living and bad weather.

“Nominal wages will rise steadily, while the pace of inflation is likely to gradually slow,” Ueda said, adding that rising household income would underpin consumption.

“We expect consumption to resume a moderate uptrend” after a temporary slowdown, he added.

On monetary policy, Ueda reiterated the central bank’s resolve to keep raising interest rates, saying financial conditions remain loose despite past hikes.

“Real interest rates in the shorter zone, which have the biggest impact on economic activity, remain low despite past rate hikes and continue to underpin growth,” Ueda said.

He also said the weak yen could have a bigger impact on inflation than in the past as firms have become more active in passing on rising costs through price hikes.

“It’s important to anchor underlying inflation around our 2 per cent target to avoid risk of an inflation overshoot from materialising and hurting the economy,” he said.

With stubbornly high energy costs and rising import prices from a weak yen adding to inflationary pressures, the BOJ raised its policy rate to 1.25 per cent in September after delivering a hike in June — a shorter interval than the roughly twice-a-year hikes in 2024 and 2025.

The central bank kept rates steady last month, declaring victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Trump hails âgreatâ ties with Xi, downplays Nvidia scandal
data.description:
[SHENZHEN] US President Donald Trump hailed his great “friendship” with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping and downplayed a spying scandal involving Nvidia, just hours before leaders of the world’s top two economies meet for talks in China.

“I was with President Xi all night last night, sitting next to him at the dinner, right on his right hand side, and we spoke the whole evening,” he told Fox News on Thursday on the sidelines of this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen.

When asked if the downfall of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, a prominent opponent of restrictions on chip sales to China, came up in conversation with Xi at a banquet on Wednesday evening, Trump said: “I might have referred to it just briefly because it’s such a tragedy.”

Trump is slated to hold his third summit of the year with Xi later on Thursday, with the fallout from the Nvidia scandal threatening to upend a fragile trade truce set to expire on Jan 10.

Washington unleashed new chip curbs earlier this week designed to thwart Beijing’s ability to train frontier artificial intelligence models, prompting Beijing to warn of countermeasures if the two sides cannot reach a resolution.

Despite the underlying tensions, Xi personally greeted Trump upon the US president’s arrival at the airport on Wednesday, returning a favour for Trump’s in-person welcome when the Chinese leader visited Washington in September.

The unusual gesture marked the first time in roughly 50 years that a Chinese leader met a visiting dignitary on the tarmac.

Trump lauded that welcome and sought to downplay reports that Huang had conducted an affair with a Chinese executive that US intelligence believes was spying for China.

“Any pretty woman that comes from China, they considered her to be a spy,” he told Fox. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips.”

Beyond the airport pageantry, expectations are low for major breakthroughs, given both leaders are meeting again at the Group of 20 leaders’ summit in Miami in December.

The two sides are looking to advance tariff reductions on US$30 billion worth of each other’s imports, negotiated under the newly established US-China Board of Trade. A similar framework has been floated for bilateral investment, though progress has been slow.

Xi urged Apec members to reduce barriers to trade and investment in his opening remarks at the leaders’ meeting on Thursday morning, calling for an “open, fair, just and non-discriminatory environment for cooperation”.

Trump and Xi are also expected to meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin this afternoon in what would be an unprecedented summit between the three men, who together control at least 90 per cent of the world’s nuclear weapons.

In 2025, Trump and Xi reached a truce to end their trade war, and agreed to extend it to early next year during their September meeting in Washington.

Under that deal, in which both sides agreed to tariff reductions, an understanding was reached for the Trump administration to hold off imposing new tech curbs against Beijing in exchange for a steady flow of critical minerals from China.

That bargain has increasingly come under strain. US officials have repeatedly complained that America is not getting rare earths at the expected volume and pace – a grievance US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer raised with Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in a video call earlier in November.

The US Commerce Department this week published interim rules that would restrict China’s remote access to high-end AI chips hosted in overseas data centers.

If thoroughly enforced, the regulation could deal a heavy blow to China’s AI ecosystem by shutting off a crucial source of computing power for Chinese developers racing to build cutting-edge models. The move drew a sharp rebuke from China’s commerce ministry.

The Xi-Trump meetings this year have been more about atmospherics and keeping the broad relationship stable than substantive negotiations on trade, investment and security matters.

Asked how the American people can tell if Thursday’s meeting is a success, Trump told Fox News: “I think I’ve already gotten that headline, because the relationship that I have with China is a great one.”

“The fanfare, the beauty, the pageantry, the thousands of people, the young children, the soldiers, the whole thing – it was a great respect, and I appreciate that,” Trump said. “That’s a big win for us. It’s a big win for China, too.” BLOOMBERG

data.title: Asiaâs family offices cool to Anthropic IPO despite strong investor demand
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Anthropic’s record-breaking US$81.3 billion initial public offering has reportedly attracted demand exceeding six times the shares on offer, but some Asia family offices are holding back, citing steep valuations and the prospect of better buying opportunities after the listing.

Despite the fanfare surrounding the landmark listing of the artificial intelligence firm, family offices and wealth advisers in Asia said that much of the company’s potential growth has already been priced in.

At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty and risks associated with the technology warrant caution, they noted.

Anthropic priced its IPO at US$83 a share on Wednesday (Nov 18), above its initial range of US$70 to US$78, valuing the AI company at about US$1.5 trillion. The company also expanded its offering to 980 million shares, up from the 825 million shares previously expected.

Anthropic’s shares are expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday.

Cameron Harvey, CEO of Hong Kong-headquartered Landmark Family Office, said that sophisticated family offices are taking a selective approach rather than chasing day-one momentum.

For investors without existing positions, the risk-reward balance favours waiting for trading activity to settle, he noted. Recent IPO performance suggests that more attractive entry points could emerge after listing.

He added that investors should pay particular attention to post-listing discovery and the expiry of lock-up periods, which could release additional shares into the market.

Arnold Ho, head of trading at Moomoo Singapore, said that demand was being driven by major institutional commitments, including reported cornerstone investments from Nvidia and Altimeter Capital, alongside strong retail interest.

Existing backers are prioritised for allocations, with some reportedly offering pre-IPO shares at a 3 to 5 per cent premium, he said, adding that the day-one float will therefore be limited.

With a limited initial free float and elevated opening demand, there could be heightened volatility and wider bid-ask spreads as the market establishes a trading price, believes Ho.

“But strong subscription demand does not guarantee that the shares will trade above the IPO price,” he cautioned.

A comparable mega-listing was SpaceX, which listed in June this year.

Its offering was more than three times oversubscribed, with shares rising 19 per cent on the first day of trading. The equity fell below its listing price of US$135 about a month later on Jul 15. It closed at US$141.70 on Tuesday.

LN Sadani, founder and CEO of Singapore-based single family office Lensbridge Capital, said that Anthropic’s competitive advantage warrants closer scrutiny than Space X’s, given the latter’s established launch and satellite infrastructure.

He pointed to the potential for open-source models to erode pricing power, and to the AI firm’s own warnings about compute dependence, harmful model behaviour and legal or regulatory exposure as some reasons for staying cautious on Anthropic.

Value created in private markets 

For some family offices, the bigger concern is that investors buying into Anthropic’s IPO may be arriving after much of the company’s valuation gains have already been realised as a private company.

Singapore sovereign wealth fund GIC has been an investor since 2025, most recently co-leading its US$65 billion fundraising in May. GIC reportedly holds about 1 per cent of the firm after investing north of US$4.5 billion in it, according to reports.

Singapore investment company Temasek has also invested in Anthropic, as part of its focus on deep-tech innovation.

“The Anthropic IPO is a landmark for private markets as much as public ones,” said Grace Tang, CEO and managing director of Phillip Private Equity.

“Most of the value creation has already happened, while the company was private. Family offices that want the next Anthropic need to be in private growth equity before the IPO, not after.”

Sadani similarly views the listing as a potential liquidity milestone for patient capital, but noted that substantial growth expectations are already reflected in private valuations.

Lensbridge Capital, however, did not invest in the pre-IPO rounds for Anthropic, as it expects more attractive opportunities to invest in the company to emerge after listing.

Broader technology sector

The listing is also being watched for its effect on the wider technology market, following a difficult month for the sector.

James Ooi, chief market strategist at Tiger Brokers, said the IPO could be an important test of market appetite for AI companies.

Meanwhile, Harvey described Anthropic – as the first frontier-AI model developer to list publicly – as a bellwether for the sector, at a time when the market is repricing future earnings assumptions.

The large raise will absorb significant institutional capital, potentially creating rotational pressure across legacy software and mega-cap tech peers as allocators rebalance their AI exposure, he noted.

Moomoo’s Ho also expects some savvy investors with concentrated exposure to semiconductor or cloud stocks to also review their positions to free up capital for Anthropic.

“However, we would not assume that clients will hedge systematically, or that the IPO will necessarily cause a liquidity drain from those stocks.”

Kam Kah Ken, CEO and chief investment officer of single family office Wellco Capital, noted that he has seen an aggressive shift of capital from AI and semiconductors into non-AI themes in recent weeks.

He nevertheless remains bullish on the sector. “Compute power is the new oil, and hyperscalers are still committed to spend (many) billions on data centres,” he said.

Geopolitics and risk disclosures

Kam added that the bigger drain on liquidity will be regulation and geopolitics, which are unfolding alongside the broader IPO market.

He highlighted the uncertainty over US restrictions on advanced AI chips, particularly their implications for South-east Asia data centres serving Chinese customers.

“Close to home, our biggest open secret is how South-east Asia regional data centres powered with advanced Nvidia chips cater to large Chinese customers like Alibaba and ByteDance,” he said.

“All the new regional data-centre builds depend on the US restricting only physical chip ownership, and not remote access by the Chinese.”

This risk has become more pressing as Washington moves to tighten restrictions on remote access to advanced AI chips, raising uncertainty over the region’s AI infrastructure expansion.

Meanwhile, Anthropic’s own risk disclosures add another layer of uncertainty for prospective shareholders.

Ooi said the extensive disclosures may introduce a dimension of uncertainty that is difficult to capture in traditional financial models.

“Investors are being asked to assess not just an emerging business model, but (also) a technology whose long-term risks and implications remain hard to quantify.”

data.title: Trump-Xi-Putin talks: US-China relations, AI chips,  Iran war among 5 things to watch
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin are meeting today in Shenzhen China for historic three-way talks.

The world’s three most powerful men and leaders from 21 Asia-Pacific economies arrived earlier for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit, with high-stakes diplomacy and economic tensions threatening to overshadow the annual meeting.

The two-day gathering, which began on Wednesday (Nov 18), comes as the US States and China navigate a fragile trade truce, Washington tightens restrictions on advanced semiconductor exports, and geopolitical disputes continue to test regional stability.

Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong is also holding a series of bilateral meetings on the sidelines.

Here are five things to watch at this year’s summit.

1. US-China relations

All eyes are on Trump and Xi as they meet in Shenzhen, with the trade truce between the world’s two largest economies due to expire in January 2027.

The two leaders last met in September in Washington, where they maintained a relatively conciliatory tone despite persistent disagreements over tariffs, technology restrictions and geopolitical issues.

Their latest meeting comes as both sides face pressure to prevent another escalation in trade tensions that could disrupt global markets and supply chains.

Xi has sought to portray China as a champion of economic openness. Speaking at the Apec CEO Summit on Wednesday, he pledged to cut tariffs, expand market access and improve conditions for foreign investors.

His remarks contrasted with Trump’s protectionist trade policies, which have raised concerns among economies dependent on international commerce.

Xi also called for closer technology partnerships and efforts to keep global supply chains and stable open.

The key question is whether the two leaders can extend their trade truce and prevent fresh disputes from undermining their relationship.

2. Lawrence Wong’s agenda

For Singapore, the summit provides an opportunity to strengthen ties with regional partners as the Republic prepares to chair Asean in 2027.

Wong began his visit on Wednesday with bilateral meetings involving Vietnamese President To Lam, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast and Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori.

The discussions covered trade, the digital economy, carbon credits and regional cooperation.

During his meeting with Lam, Wong highlighted opportunities for Singapore and Vietnam to support each other’s priorities next year, when Singapore chairs Asean and Vietnam chairs Apec.

He also discussed strengthening economic cooperation with Chile and Peru, including through existing trade agreements and new opportunities in the digital economy.

Wong said Singapore hoped to deepen collaboration with its partners amid growing global uncertainty.

Wong is scheduled to address the Apec leaders’ meeting on Thursday and meet Xi on Friday, before travelling to Beijing for talks with Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Saturday.

His engagements with China’s top leaders will be closely watched for indications of how Singapore intends to strengthen bilateral economic ties while navigating growing rivalry between major powers.

3. US-China chip, AI race

The US-China technology rivalry has intensified just days before the summit, following Washington’s announcement of tighter restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

The new measures, announced on Monday, require export licences for certain advanced semiconductors shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil.

They also target overseas data centres that provide significant computing capacity to Chinese companies, as Washington seeks to prevent Beijing from circumventing existing export controls.

China has criticised the restrictions as economic coercion and warned that it would take necessary measures to protect its interests.

The move threatens to complicate Trump-Xi talks, particularly as access to advanced chips remains central to both countries’ ambitions in AI.

The restrictions also have implications for Singapore, a major semiconductor trading hub and growing data centre market.

Wong said on Tuesday that Singapore could manage the impact on chips transhipped through the Republic, but was more concerned about those used by local companies and data centres.

Still, Singapore is pressing ahead with three national AI missions for financial services.

Whether Washington and Beijing can prevent their technology rivalry from escalating further will be a key development to watch.

Rare earths - crucial for the clean energy transition and electric vehicles - may also be discussed. The global supply is currently dominated by China and the US is struggling to catch up. On Tuesday, Trump gave a 10-month time frame, which analysts said is unlikely to happen.

4. Putin’s presence and geopolitics

Putin’s attendance marks his first in-person appearance at an Apec leaders’ meeting since 2017.

He is expected to join Trump and Xi for a three-way meeting on Thursday, bringing together the leaders of three major nuclear powers.

Trump has previously floated denuclearisation as a possible discussion topic, although China has historically resisted negotiations over nuclear stockpile limits with Russia and the US, which possess much larger arsenals.

The meeting also takes place against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine and the conflict involving Iran.

A senior US administration official said Trump intended to discuss Iran with the two leaders but was not expected to raise Ukraine.

Putin used his address to the Apec CEO Summit on Wednesday to criticise Western sanctions and export restrictions, while highlighting Russia’s growing economic ties with the Asia-Pacific.

He said trade with the region now accounts for more than half of Russia’s total trade.

His presence gives Moscow an opportunity to deepen engagement with Asian economies despite Western efforts to isolate Russia following its invasion of Ukraine.

5. Regional disputes

Although Apec is primarily an economic forum, the gathering comes amid persistent security tensions in the Asia-Pacific.

Among the most contentious issues are competing territorial claims in the South China Sea, where China and several South-east Asian countries, including the Philippines and Vietnam, have overlapping claims.

The disputes have complicated efforts by Asean and China to conclude a Code of Conduct governing behaviour in the contested waters.

The Philippines ended its Asean chairmanship this week without securing a final agreement on the code, leaving the issue unresolved as Singapore prepares to take over the grouping’s leadership. The unfinished maritime negotiations remain among the key challenges facing the region.

Security concerns also extend to the Korean Peninsula, where North Korea’s nuclear weapons and missile programmes continue to unsettle neighbouring countries.

While such issues are not expected to dominate Apec’s formal economic discussions, they could feature in bilateral meetings and informal exchanges among leaders.

For Singapore, regional stability is closely linked to economic confidence and trade, making developments in the South China Sea and wider Asia-Pacific particularly significant.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Jardine Matheson, Riverstone, Deluge
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Wednesday (Nov 18):

Jardine Matheson: The Hong Kong-based conglomerate expects to post a 2026 dividend of at least US$2.50 per share, amid “strong performance” for the third quarter ended Sep 30. This comes after Jardine Matheson raised its full-year profit guidance in October to between US$5.50 and US$5.65 per share on an underlying basis, from the previous guidance of US$5.33 per share. For Q3, its Indonesian unit Astra International’s underlying net profit rose 11 per cent. Shares of Jardine Matheson closed 1 per cent or US$0.62 lower at US$59.15 on Tuesday, before the news.

Riverstone : The glove maker posted a 34.7 per cent rise in net profit to RM70.1 million (US$17.1 million) for the third quarter ended September. Riverstone’s Q3 revenue rose 27.3 per cent to RM315.1 million, marking the group’s highest quarterly revenue in over three years. It also announced that CEO Wong Teek Son will step down on Dec 1, to be succeeded by Chong Chu Mee. Riverstone shares closed 2.1 per cent or S$0.015 higher at S$0.745 on Tuesday, before the results.

Deluge : The fire detection and protection company has secured S$18.5 million in new contracts across Singapore and Malaysia, bringing its cumulative contract wins since January 2026 to more than S$147.7 million. The latest awards span infrastructure, marine and offshore, residential and industrial projects, including a Penang data centre project. Shares of Deluge closed 0.8 per cent or S$0.005 lower at S$0.605 on Tuesday.
